seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I owe you an apology for my delay in answering your letters. Your friends in Venice sent me the name of the oculist (Dr Haab). Please thank Mrs Pound for her kindness in writing to them about me. The card came this afternoon but in the morning I had been to Dr Sidler (Dr. Haab’s brother-in-law who with him directs the Augenklinik here). I imagine there cannot be a great difference therefore between the two opinions except that Dr Sidler’s fee is somewhat less. He says he thinks an operation is unavoidable but as the pressure is not so great in the eye now he wants to wait a fortnight. He says however that I must not go in the country (which I had no intention of doing) as immediately I have any bad symptoms I must have a doctor at hand. He thinks also that the climate here is bad for me. He spoke about testing my blood. I asked can synechia be cured without iridectomy. He said not. I should like to wait if I can for Dr Gould’s opinion. Forgive me therefore if I am not a very good letter writer at present.

I hope your new review is a success. Miss Monro Monroe
writes me that she likes the verses I sent and will print them in Poetry so that I suppose they will not appear in your pages. I hope I shall be able to send you something else instead. I am not allowed to write much because my eye becomes hard if I strain it. As regards Ulysses I managed to finish the draft of Hades’ house and also the lotuseaters and am getting together the notes for the Eolian episode.

I had to interrupt this letter on account of a violent thunderstorm and I resume it with gastric cramps resultant therefrom. Like Mr Maeterlinck’s heroine I am not brave. Please convey to Mr de Bosschère my thanks for his good opinion of my book. Perhaps he will review it for some French paper? I hear that a second edition came out in New York a month ago but I do not know how many copies were in the first edition. Has Mr Quinn received my play ? I do not know whether the Stage Society is putting it on or not.

I hope you are well and in your usual admirable good humour. I hope also that you will come here on your way to the south. I should be very glad indeed to see you. Please let me know if you think of coming here during the next months.
My wife bids me thank you for your letter, with its encouraging references to my novel with the concertina title, and joins me in sending to Mrs Pound and yourself all friendly regards.

div.note: Pound had written to JJ on 19 April and 18 May 1917, and to Nora Barnacle on 7 and 14 May 1917 while JJ was indisposed with eye trouble (Pound/Joyce 110-18).

Dorothy Pound, née Shakespear (1886-1973), English artist who married Pound in London in April 1914. Writing JJ on 27 June 1917, Pound commented on efforts to find a proper eye specialist: “I trust a good deal to old Eden having been ready to go to Zurich” (Pound/Joyce 120). Dorothy and her mother, the novelist Olivia Shakespear, had travelled in Italy before World War I and had become friends with an English couple named Eden who resided in Venice. Olivia dedicated her novel, Uncle Hilary (1910), “To my friend Frederic Eden.” Scholars have identified this figure as the Reverend Frederick Nugent Eden (1857-1926), an Anglican clergyman (John Harwood, Olivia Shakespear and W.B. Yeats: After Long Silence [New York: St. Martin’s Press, 1989], 123, 204 n.29), but this is incorrect. The Frederic Eden (1829-1916) whom Dorothy knew was the well-known English author of A Garden in Venice (1903) and designer of a celebrated garden on the island of Giudecca in Venice, where he and his wife entertained writers and artists at their villa. This is clear from a March 1910 letter in which Pound told his mother that in Venice “the Shakespears [Dorothy and Olivia] usuly [sic] put up at the Edens – (of the Venetian Garden)” (Ezra Pound to his Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 225). In a March 1914 letter to Dorothy, Pound referred to “old Eden” in Venice, who had given her a wedding gift of £20 (Ezra Pound and Dorothy Shakespear: Their Letters, 1909-1914, ed. Omar Pound and A. Walton Litz [New York: New Directions, 1984], 323). The difficulty here is that the Frederic Eden of the Venice garden appears to have died in December 1916, so it is unclear exactly who the “old Eden” was who was willing to go to Zurich to assist JJ in 1917. Perhaps Pound had misunderstood. In any case, JJ’s phrase “Your friends in Venice” almost certainly refers to the Eden family in Venice whom Dorothy knew and must have contacted for JJ.

Otto Haab (1850-1931) directed the eye clinic (Augenklinik) of the University of Zurich from 1885 to 1919. He was succeeded as director by Ernst Sidler-Huguenin (1869-1922), who in turn was succeeded by Alfred Vogt (1879-1943). All three of these professors of ophthalmology treated JJ’s eyes.

For synechia, see JJ to Pound, 13 April 1917, notes. JJ suffered a severe attack of glaucoma in August 1917, prompting his ophthalmologist, Ernst Sidler, to perform an iridectomy on his right eye at the Zurich Augenklinik a few days later. Resulting exudation from the eye during convalescence permanently reduced JJ’s vision (Ellmann, JJ 417).

George Milbry Gould (1848-1922), a noted ophthalmologist and prolific author who practiced in Philadelphia before settling in Ithaca, NY, and Atlantic City, NJ, in later years. Pound had been treated by Gould some years before this, and felt that he might be able to help JJ. For a full account, see JJ to Pound, 13 April 1917, notes.

For two years, Pound had been casting about for a magazine to edit with John Quinn’s financial support. Quinn agreed to help underwrite Pound’s role as foreign editor of The Little Review, and Pound announced in the May 1917 issue that he viewed the magazine as “a place where the current prose writings of James Joyce, Wyndham Lewis, T.S. Eliot, and myself might appear regularly, promptly, and together, rather than irregularly, sporadically, and after useless delays” (Little Review, vol. 4, no. 1 [May 1917]: 3). See also JJ to Pound, 13 April 1917, notes.

Harriet Monroe (1860-1936) was editor of the Chicago-based magazine Poetry, which she launched in 1912 with financial support from local business leaders. Monroe published JJ’s poems “Simples,” “Tutto è Sciolto,” “Flood,” “A Flower Given to My Daughter,” and “Nightpiece” as a group in the May 1917 issue of Poetry, and “On the Beach at Fontana,” “Alone,” and “She Weeps over Rahoon” in the November 1917 issue. These poems, with revisions, were all collected in Pomes Penyeach (1927).

“Lotus-Eaters,” “Hades,” and “Aeolus” are, respectively, the fifth, sixth, and seventh episodes of Ulysses (1922), initially published serially in the July, September, and October 1918 numbers of The Little Review in New York. “Hades” was also published serially in The Egoist in London in the numbers for July and September 1919.

Possibly a reference to the play Princess Maleine (1889) by the Belgian author Maurice Maeterlinck (1862-1949). During Act II when she meets Prince Hjalmar in a wood at night, Maleine repeatedly murmurs, “I am afraid.” Thunderstorms are frequent in the play, and Maleine is murdered during one of them. JJ was morbidly fearful of thunderstorms throughout his life.

Jean de Bosschère (1878-1953), Belgian artist and author, moved to London during World War I and there met Pound and other avant-garde writers. Pound helped to place his poems and drawings in The Little Review and promoted his work in other ways. In a letter to Nora Barnacle dated 7 May 1917, Pound quoted Bosschère’s praise for A Portrait as being free from “tout ornement rhétorique” and being “l’oeuvre le plus sérieux en anglais que j’ai lu” (free of “all rhetorical ornament” and “the most serious work in English I have read”) (Pound/Joyce 114-15).

B.W. Huebsch of New York first issued A Portrait as a book in December 1916 in an edition of unascertained size. He produced a second printing in April 1917 (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 18).
On 13 May 1917, JJ wrote John Quinn – who was seeking to purchase manuscripts by JJ – that he had sent him (through Pound) the manuscript of Exiles (LII 396).

Founded in 1899, the London-based Incorporated Stage Society presented new, experimental, and sometimes controversial plays, including those by George Bernard Shaw, W.B. Yeats, Henrik Ibsen, and Gerhart Hauptmann. Shaw, J.M. Barrie, and others were officials of the company, which staged private performances of plays that had been denied a license for public performance by the Lord Chamberlain. The Society considered Exiles during 1916 and 1917 but in the end did not mount it, possibly because of disagreement over certain “tabooed” words, as Shaw later suggested (Ellmann, JJ 443 n.). The Society finally presented Exiles at London’s Regent Theatre on 14 and 15 February 1926, with W.G. Fay as director.

Pound had written Nora Barnacle on 7 May 1917: “I shall go to the Lago di Garda after the war, unless I am destroyed, and I shall manage to pass through Zurich or Italy redeemed or wherever J.J. is at that time” (Pound/Joyce 115). Pound had first stayed at Sirmione on Lago di Garda in northern Italy in 1910. With its literary associations going back to Catullus, the lake became for Pound a mystical, paradisal spot and is a recurrent setting in his Cantos and other poems. In his early poem “The Flame,” Pound wrote of Lake Garda: “Who can look on that blue and not believe?” (Personae: The Shorter Poems, ed. Lea Baechler and A. Walton Litz [New York: New Directions, 1990], 49). He revisited the lake in later years, and first met JJ there in June 1920.

Pound had written Nora Barnacle on 7 May 1917 of his and others’ admiration for A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (“the concertina title”), adding: “I dont know what the press can say that they haven’t said already. So far as press notices can make a book, the ‘Portrait’ is ‘made.’ And J.J. may derive what satisfaction he can from it. He knew the work was good, or at least he ought to have known, if he didn’t” (Pound/Joyce 115).
